newsitem.title: USA: BP discovery poses environmental questions.
newsitem.headline: BP discovery poses environmental questions.

text.p: Discovery of oil on the border of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge (ANWR) raised hopes among business leaders and politicians, but environmentalists on Friday voiced fears about oil development within the reserve.

British Petroleum's BP Exploration Inc and Chevron's Chevron USA announced the discovery of a possible 100-million-barrel oil reserve at their Sourdough prospect on Thursday. The find was about 50 miles (80 km) east of Prudhoe Bay and on a state lease near the North Slope's Canning River, BP said.
Some Alaska politicians hailed the oil find as justification to open the Arctic wildlife refuge to drilling, an idea vehemently opposed by the Clinton administration.

"It cast even greater pressure now on the administration to recognise that this whole area of northern Alaska...it is a must that this area be explored," Sen. Ted Stevens, an Alaska Republican, told Anchorage radio station KSKA.

Some environmentalists said they were relieved the discovery was not as large as had been rumoured. "The strike itself if pretty small. It's really no big deal, per se," said Jack Hession, Alaska representative to the Sierra Club.
Hession said the area was important for migrating caribou and should be protected. "We will be working to ensure that the spillover effects, if any, will be minimised, or not even allowed," he said.

U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt said federal officials would also scrutinise the development to ensure that the wildlife refuge was protected. Protection includes ensuring that oil from beneath the refuge was not drained off by adjacent wells, he said in a statement on Thursday.
But Bob King, spokesman for Democratic Gov. Tony Knowles, played down the link between Sourdough and drilling in the refuge.

"I don't think there are any ANWR implications. I think the only impact on ANWR development is that the governor believes this gives us another opportunity to show that we can do (development) right," King said.

BP -- which has done extensive seismic work in the area and drilled previous wells -- plans to drill a delineation well at the prospect next winter to get a better idea of the size of the reserve and the economic feasibility of production, said company spokesman Paul Laird.
If the site is developed, modern technology would mitigate the impact on the area, he said.
"The impact of development of Sourdough would be minimal, and anyway, it's state land. That's the bottom line," Laird said.

Fears that Sourdough's developers might siphon off federal oil through angled drilling are addressed by state laws, Laird said. The state requires a buffer when wells are placed near the edge of property boundaries and forbids extraction of oil from outside designated units, he said.
BP has always promoted ANWR development, "But Sourdough is not a back-door approach to getting into ANWR," Laird said.
